title: A soft answer (Proverbs 15:1; 18:21)
hookLine: a soft answer turns away wrath; death and life are in the tongue
last: A LITTLE FOLDING OF THE HANDS.

lines: PROVERBS HAS ONE LINE FOR THIS.
cards: The text arrives at 11:40 at night. It's from a brother, and it starts with the words "so apparently." Three replies get drafted in the head, each sharper than the last, and the best one is really good.
It would land. It would win. A thumb hovers over the screen.
It's an old moment, much older than phones, and the people who collected the sayings in the book of Proverbs knew it too. They didn't write a rule for it.
They wrote a single line, short enough to remember with your pulse up.

teach.h: STILL AN ANSWER, JUST A SOFT ONE.
teach.b: Proverbs chapter fifteen opens with it, in the King James Bible: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." Notice what it doesn't say: stay quiet, or agree, or let them walk all over you.
It's still an answer. You still speak.
The Hebrew is ma'aneh rakh: a reply that is tender, gentle, the way you'd handle something easily bruised. The proverb is about the temperature of the words, not whether you get to say them.
And it's practical, almost sly. Anger needs something to push against. A grievous word, a word that hurts, hands the other person a wall to push.
A soft one gives them nothing to push on, and the anger often runs out of road.

teach.h: A SOFT TONGUE BREAKS THE BONE.
teach.b: Chapter twenty-five says it even more strangely: "a soft tongue breaketh the bone." Softness, in Proverbs, isn't weakness. It's what gets through.

teach.h: DEATH AND LIFE ARE IN THE TONGUE.
teach.b: Then chapter eighteen raises the stakes: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof." Words aren't air.

They build or they wreck, and whoever loves to talk will eat whatever they've been planting. The letter of James spends much of a chapter on the tongue, calling it a little fire that can set a great deal alight.

teach.h: A SOFT ANSWER TURNETH AWAY WRATH.
teach.b: Proverbs doesn't promise the soft answer always works. Some people stay angry. It just says which way the odds lean, and which words you'll be eating later.

how: Many Christians memorize Proverbs 15:1 and return to it in family life and at work; it is often taught to children as a first verse about how to speak, and the book of Proverbs is read straight through in some churches, a chapter a day.

o: silent, choosing to say nothing back at all
soft, tender, like something easily bruised
agreeing quickly so the fight is over

games.q: what's inside the proverbs — tap the pairs.

s: the proverb says to stay silent when someone is angry
it's still an answer. the proverb is about how soft the words are, not whether you speak.
Proverbs says a soft tongue can break a bone
"a soft tongue breaketh the bone" — gentleness, in Proverbs, is what gets through.
Proverbs promises a soft answer always calms people down
it says which way the odds lean, not that every angry person will listen.

games.q: someone fires an angry message at you, and the perfect cutting reply is ready. what does Proverbs 15:1 point you to?
o: send the cutting reply: they started it.
answer, but softly, saying what you mean at a lower temperature.
games.why: "a soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." it's still an answer. the surprise is that the gentle one is the one that gets through.

practice: Bring to mind a conversation that tends to heat up, hear the line that usually starts it, and notice your body's first move: the jaw, the shoulders, the quick reply forming.
Now, without rushing, find a softer answer, not a surrender, the same truth at a lower temperature, and say it silently until it feels like yours. If you pray, you can hold that person before God.

wordCard.voice: Rakh. The Hebrew word for something soft or delicate, used in a proverb that says a gentle reply can turn anger away.

orig.note: Hebrew: a tender, gentle reply. rakh is the word for something soft or delicate.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing to push on. A soft answer is still an answer. Day four hundred fifty-two.
